Objective Bisphenol A glycidyl methacrylate (Bis-GMA) is of great importance for dental materials as the preferred monomer. However, the presence of bisphenol-A (BPA) core in Bis-GMA structure causes potential concerns since it is associated with endocrine diseases, developmental abnormalities, and cancer lesions. Therefore, it is desirable to develop an alternative replacement for Bis-GMA and explore the intrinsic relationship between monomer structure and resin properties.
Methods Here, the betulin maleic diester derivative (MABet) was synthesized by a facile esterification reaction using plant-derived betulin and maleic anhydride as raw materials. Its chemical structure was confirmed by 1H and 13C NMR spectra, FT-IR spectra, and HR-MS, respectively. The as-synthesized MABet was then used as polymerizable comonomer to partially or completely substitute Bis-GMA in a 50:50 Bis-GMA: TEGDMA resin (5B5T) to formulate dental restorative resins. These were then determined for the viscosity behavior, light transmittance, real-time degree of conversion, residual monomers, mechanical performance, cytotoxicity, and antibacterial activity against Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) in detail.
Results Among all experimental resins, increasing the MABet concentration to 50 wt% made the resultant 5MABet5T resin have a maximum in viscosity and appear dark yellowish after polymerization. In contrast, the 1MABet4B5T resin with 10 wt% MABet possessed comparable shear viscosity and polymerization conversion (46.6 ± 1.0% in 60 s), higher flexural and compressive strength (89.7 ± 7.8 MPa; 345.5 ± 14.4 MPa) to those of the 5B5T control (48.5 ± 0.6%; 65.7 ± 6.7 MPa; 223.8 ± 57.1 MPa). This optimal resin also had significantly lower S. mutans colony counts (0.35 ×108 CFU/mL) than 5B5T (7.6 ×108 CFU/mL) without affecting cytocompatibility.
Significance Introducing plant-derived polymerizable MABet monomer into dental restorative resins is an effective strategy for producing antibacterial dental materials with superior physicochemical property.

ce:abstract-sec.ce:simple-para: Bisphenol A glycidyl methacrylate (Bis-GMA) is of great importance for dental materials as the preferred monomer. ce:section.ce:para: Nowadays, dental caries remains one of the most prevalent non-communicable diseases and poses serious global public health burden [1,2]. Various restorative materials are available to replace the structure of decayed teeth [3], where resin-based composites have gained much attention in clinical practice due to their fascinating features, such as natural esthetics and excellent biocompatibility, and therefore represent as a popular choice for patients and dentists [4,5]. Generally, methacrylate chemistry serves as the foundation for the organic matrix since 1960 s, where the degree of cross-linking of multiple methacrylates is essential for composite performance [6,7]. Bisphenol A glycerolate dimethacrylate (Bis-GMA) is the preferred monomer utilized as the foundation for dental resin formulations due to its rigid bisphenol-A (BPA) core and two pendant hydroxyl groups, resulting in high viscosity (η = 1200 Pa.s) and low reaction mobility during the photo-polymerization [8]. In addition, the presence of BPA causes potential concerns since it is associated with various endocrine diseases, developmental abnormalities, and cancer lesions [9–11]. Although current research indicates that the short-term risk of estrogenic effects from Bis-GMA-based restorations is negligible [12], it is prudent to develop alternative replacements as a means of mitigating any possible safety risks associated with their long-term utilization and possible release of contaminants.

Plant-derived natural products are highly attractive due to their biocompatibility, biosafety, and multiple reactive groups that can be used for polymerizable functionalization [13–15]. Bioactive properties of natural products, including antibacterial and anti-inflammatory effects [16–18], make them interesting candidates for the design and preparation of multifunctional monomers for dental composite applications. For example, eugenol obtained from Eugenia caryophyllata could be functionalized with polymerizable methacrylate groups via Fisher esterification reaction [19]. The as-synthesized eugenol derivatives exhibited antibacterial activity against Streptococcus mutans (S. mutans) and good cellular proliferation, indicating that they were potentially efficacious for dental materials. Multi-methacrylated bile acid derivatives with adjustable viscosity, hydrophobicity, and reactivity were prepared and investigated for the effect of chemical structure on the degree of conversion, polymerization shrinkage, and the mechanical performance of the resulting polymers and dental composites [17]. Two dimethacrylate monomers derived from bio-based creosol were synthesized and further used to prepare the Bis-GMA-free resin matrix and resin composites to eliminate estrogenic activity [20]. These composites had higher double bond conversion, lower volumetric shrinkage, and lower cytotoxicity than those of Bis-GMA-based materials. Other bio-sourced chemicals, such as limonene and isosorbide, have also been reported as promising alternatives to BPA for the development of polymerizable monomers due to their rigidity and transparency [21,22]. In our previous work, betulin, a naturally occurring triterpene isolated from the bark of birch trees, was successfully introduced to develop mono- and di-methacrylated betulin derivatives (M1Bet and M2Bet) as antibacterial comonomers for dental resins [23]. Results showed that 10 wt% M2Bet made the resulting resin possess higher transparency, improved polymerization rate, and lower S. mutans colony counts. However, the antibacterial activity should be further increased. In terms of chemical structures, the presence of COOH or COO- groups in monomers can influence the antibacterial property of the resulting resin materials through factors such as membrane disruption [24,25], electrostatic interactions [26,27], and improved surface wettability [28,29], thus affecting the growth and viability of microorganisms. In addition, the relationship between the polymerizable structures of carboxyl-containing monomers and the physical-chemical properties of the resultant dental resins remains to be elucidated.

In this work, the betulin maleic diester derivative (MABet) was synthesized by the facile esterification reaction between betulin and maleic anhydride, where the filtration process was used to isolate and purify the product. The obtained MABet further served as a substitute for Bis-GMA in resin mixtures. The rheology behavior, light transmittance, conversion degree, mechanical performance, cytotoxicity, and antibacterial property of various resin formulations were explored in detail. All results were also compared to a Bis-GMA/TEGDMA (50/50, wt/wt) control. The objective of this work is to develop an alternative replacement for Bis-GMA and to explore the intrinsic relationship between monomer structure and resin properties. The introduction of MABet monomer into dental restorative resins should be an effective strategy for producing antibacterial dental materials with superior physicochemical property. The hypothesis is that higher MABet content produces dental resins with higher antibacterial activity at the detriment of light transmittance, polymerization conversion, and mechanical performance.

Maleic anhydride (≥99%), 4-dimethylaminopyridine (DMAP, ≥99%), and triethylamine (TEA, ≥99%) were purchased from Macklin Biochemical Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Bisphenol A glycerolate dimethacrylate (Bis-GMA, >98%), camphorquinone (CQ, 97%), tri(ethyleneglycol) dimethacrylate (TEGDMA, 95%), and ethyl-4-dimethylaminobenzoate (4-EDMAB, 99%) were received from Sigma-Aldrich. ce:section.ce:para: The control resin is comprised of photo-initiators (0.2 wt% CQ and 0.8 wt% 4-EDMAB) and resin monomers (50 wt% Bis-GMA and 50 wt% TEGDMA) [9,20], abbreviated as 5B5T. The as-synthesized MABet was used to partially or completely substitute Bis-GMA with various adding quantities of 10, 30, or 50 wt% relative to the total amount of dental resins, and the resulting resins are named as 1MABet4B5T, 3MABet2B5T, and 5MABet5T, respectively. All dental resin mixtures were prepared with a Speedmixer (DAC 150.1 FVZ-K, Germany). The obtained resin pastes were put into the through-hole silicone rubber molds covering the top and bottom with glass slides and irradiated for 60 s on each side with an LED curing lamp (SLC-8D, 430–490 nm, China).

1H and 13C NMR spectra of MABet and betulin in CDCl3 were determined on a Bruker AVANCE III HD400 spectrometer. Their attenuated total reflection Fourier transform infrared (ATR-FT-IR) spectra were recorded on a Bruker Nicolet 8700 spectrometer in the range of 4000–400 cm−1 with a resolution of 4 cm−1. The high-resolution mass spectrum (HR-MS) of MABet was obtained by a Waters G2-XS QToF spectrometer (ion source: ESI).
(1) Rheology property.

The viscosity of dental resins without photo-initiators was measured by a modular rheometer device (MCR-302, Anton Paar, Austria) with a 25 mm parallel plate. During the tests, each resin (0.5 mL) was put onto the plate. Steady shear sweep tests were performed to evaluate the shear viscosity at 37 °C along the shear rates from 0.1 to 100 1/s.
(2) Light transmittance.
Disk samples (Φ 10 mm × 1 mm) of each resin were made and their transmittance characteristics from 250 to 500 nm were evaluated by a UV–vis–NIR spectrophotometer (UV3600, Shimadzu, Japan).
(3) Real-time polymerization conversion.

The real-time assessment of the degree of CC double bond conversion was determined by an FT-IR spectrometer (Nicolet 8700, Germany) with an ATR mold. A small sample (5 µL, n = 3) was placed on the ATR unit and the infrared spectrum was recorded. Then, the resin sample was light-cured for total 10 min and FT-IR spectra were taken every 10 s for the first 2 min and every 40 s for the last 8 min. To evaluate the polymerization conversion of dental resins containing Bis-GMA (5B5T, 1MABet4B5T, and 3MABet2B5T), the heights of absorbance peaks of an aliphatic CC band at 1638 cm−1 and an aromatic CC band at 1608 cm−1 (the internal standard) were measured and compared, respectively. (4) Analysis of residual monomers.

Disk-shaped specimens (15 mm × 1 mm, n = 3) of each dental resin were made and transferred into the 30 mL amber colored vials containing 75% ethanol solution for extraction, where the ratio of samples to solution was 1:20. After 24 h of immersion, the specimen was removed and the extraction was rotary evaporated. The residual unreacted monomers in the polymerized resin specimens were determined with 1H NMR spectroscopy (Bruker AVANCE III HD400, Germany) in CDCl3. In addition, MABet, Bis-GMA, and TEGDMA were used as standard monomers for analysis.
(5) Mechanical performance.

For the measurement of flexural strength and modulus, six bar-shaped samples for each resin formulation were made at a size of 25 mm × 2 mm × 2 mm. Next, for compressive testing, six cylindrical samples (Φ 4 mm × 6 mm) were prepared. Three-point bending tests were performed to determine flexural properties and compressive strength of dental resin samples using a universal testing machine (Instron 33 R 4201, USA) at a cross-head speed of 0.75 mm/min [18]. In addition, flexural and compressive properties of all these resins were also assessed in wet conditions after immersion in distilled water at 37 ℃ for 24 h, according to ISO 4049–2009 [31].
(6) In vitro cytotoxicity (CCK-8 assay).

Human dental pulp cells (HDPCs) were selected in this work and the in vitro cytotoxicity of dental resins was determined by the CCK-8 tests. Round-shaped discs (Φ 10 mm × 1 mm, n = 6) from each resin were made and their extracts were prepared according to our reported studies [18,23]. Each extract was diluted to 50% with DMEM, transferred to 96-well plates containing 1 × 103 cells/well, and incubated for 1, 3, and 5 days, respectively. After each incubation period, the optical density of every well was measured by a microplate reader (Elx800, USA) at a wavelength of 450 nm. Additionally, HDPCs were stained with a calcein-AM/PI kit and the cell morphology was detected by a fluorescence microscope (Leica DMi8, Germany).
(7) Antibacterial property.

The plate-counting method was carried out to assess the antibacterial property of dental resins using S. mutans (ATCC 25175) as the representative bacterial strain. Bacterial suspensions were prepared according to our previous work [32,33] and then added to each disk-shaped resin sample (Φ 30 mm × 1 mm, n = 3) [23]. After 24 h of anaerobic incubation at 37 ℃, 8 mL PBS was added into each well and the obtained bacterial suspension was serially diluted with BHI broth. Afterwards, 100 µL of each suspension was inoculated on BHIA plate for 48 h. The number of bacteria was counted and CFU counts were evaluated. Furthermore, the bacterial morphology grown onto dental resins were investigated by a confocal laser scanning microscope (CLSM, Olympus FV1200, Japan) and a field emission scanning electron microscope (FE-SEM, SU8010, Japan), respectively.
Statistical significance was performed by one-way analysis of variance together with Tukey’s tests using the SPSS version 20.0 (IBM Corp., USA). The significance level was set at p < 0.05.

The typical 1H NMR spectra of compounds are shown in Fig. 1(a). The signal of the proton on C19 of betulin and MABet is distinctly visible at 2.40 ppm and therefore serves as a reference. The 1H signal at 3.21 ppm corresponds to the proton of C3, while 3.35 and 3.82 ppm represent the proton of C28 of betulin. After reacting with malic anhydride, MABet was synthesized via the esterification (Fig. 1a inset). The protons attached to betulin adjacent to both alcohols move downfield due to the formation of ester bonds, indicating their conjugation. The featured proton resonance signals at 6.49 and 6.40 ppm may be assigned to the protons of the CH=CH of the maleic anhydride, suggesting the presence of maleic acid. The 13C NMR spectra of the compounds are displayed in Fig. 1(b). The resonance signals of C3 and C28 have undergone a shift from 79.02 and 60.52 ppm to 84.78 and 65.57 ppm, respectively, further demonstrating the establishment of ester bonds. The presence of new signals at 167.95, 167.62, 165.26, and 164.93 ppm could be assigned to the carboxyl carbon, while 136.21, 135.62, 129.81, and 129.47 ppm correspond to the methine carbon of the maleic acid molecule. The monomer structure is further confirmed by FTIR (Fig. 1c) and HR-MS (Fig. 1d). Compared with the FTIR spectrum of betulin (Fig. 1c), the absorption peak of the -OH at 3443 cm−1 disappears in MABet. Instead, new absorption bands at 1711 and 1164 cm−1 are found in MABet, which are ascribed from CO and C-O of ester group. As seen in Fig. 1(d), the mass of MABet (C38H54O8) is observed for 637.3741 m/z [M-H]-, which is calculated for 638.3819 m/z. These results indicate that MABet was synthesized successfully.

The effect of the as-synthesized MABet on the shear viscosity of resin mixtures was investigated and the results are compared with 5B5T (Fig. 2a). All studied dental resins exhibit a pseudoplastic shear thinning behavior. Indeed, the partial or total substitution of Bis-GMA by MABet changes the flowability of resin formulations. As the concentration of MABet gradually increases from 10 to 50 wt%, the 5MABet5T resin can produce a maximum in viscosity, followed by 3MABet2B5T and 1MABet4B5T. Among these resins, only the 1MABet4B5T resin exhibits the comparable viscosity to the control resin (5B5T), achieving the desired flow behavior. Furthermore, although MABet is a light-yellow powder compared to Bis-GMA (viscous, honey-like liquid) [34], it is miscible with methacrylated-based resins, which can be clearly found from their digital photos (Fig. 2b).

The light spectra through dental resins are plotted as a function of wavelength ( Fig. 3a). It is seen that all formulated resins exhibit significantly lower transmittance compared with 5B5T. Furthermore, as seen in Fig. 3(b), increasing the concentration of MABet from 10 to 50 wt% significantly decreases the light transmittance value of the corresponding 1MABet4B5T, 3MABet2B5T, and 5MABet5T resins from 68.5 to 10.3% at the maximum absorption wavelength of CQ (λmax = 468 nm) [35]. The digital images of these polymerized resins also confirm these results (Fig. 3c). It is obviously found that MABet-based resins appear from pale yellowish to dark yellowish with increasing MABet content.

The reaction extent versus light-curing time of the developed resins containing MABet compared with 5B5T is presented in Fig. 3(d, e). A rapid increase in polymerization conversion of all resin mixtures occurs within the first 120 s, and then gradually enters a stable state until 600 s (Fig. 3d). Among all materials, the 5B5T resin exhibits the maximum conversion values at each time point, whereas the 1MABet4B5T resin containing only 10 wt% MABet demonstrates a similar polymerization behavior. In contrast, an apparent delay in polymerization kinetics is identified for 3MABet2B5T and 5MABet5T, and the delay is extended with the MABet concentration. The polymerization conversion values of 5B5T, 1MABet4B5T, 3MABet2B5T, and 5MABet5T at 60 s is measured as 48.5 ± 0.6%, 46.6 ± 1.0%, 41.8 ± 0.3%, and 4.6 ± 1.1%, respectively, and only 1MABet4B5T is comparable to 5B5T (Fig. 3e).

ce:section.ce:section-title: Analysis of residual monomers in dental resins
ce:section.ce:para: The 1H NMR spectra of the extraction of the studied dental resins are shown in Fig. 4. On the basis of 5B5T, the characteristic peaks of residual Bis-GMA (purple color) and TEGDMA (blue color) are detected. Similarly, for 1MABet4B5T and 3MABet2B5T, MABet is also found as the unreacted monomer (green color) apart from Bis-GMA and TEGDMA. In terms of 5MABet5T, residual MABet and TEGDMA are observed.

The flexural properties and compressive strength of dental resins are exhibited in Fig. 5(a-c). It is observed that the MABet concentration in resin mixtures affects their mechanical performance. Before immersion in water, among three experimental groups, the 1MABet4B5T resin possesses significantly higher flexural strength (89.7 ± 7.8 MPa) and compressive strength (345.5 ± 14.4 MPa) than the 3MABet2B5T and 5MABet5T groups (Fig. 5a, c), respectively. There is no statistical difference in the flexural modulus between different resin mixtures (Fig. 5b). More importantly, the 10 wt% addition of MABet produces the optimal 1MABet4B5T resin with better reinforcing effect in contrast with 5B5T, giving improvements of 36.5, 27.3, 54.4% for flexural strength, modulus, and compressive strength (Fig. 5a-c), respectively. The strain-stress curves demonstrate that the fracture strength of both 1MABet4B5T and 5B5T resins is higher than that of the other two resins (Fig. 5d). In addition, all these formulated resins show somewhat decreased mechanical properties after immersion in water for 24 h (Fig. 5a-c).

The optical density at 450 nm (OD450) of dental resins as a function of the incubation time is presented in Fig. 6(a), which is used as an indicator of cell viability. The OD values of all groups are gradually increased with the prolongation of culture time except 5MABet5T. Additionally, the 1MABet4B5T resin exhibits better cytocompatibility than 3MABet2B5T, which is also comparable to 5B5T. The cell morphology grown onto these resins was assessed by fluorescence microscopy (Fig. 6b). A progressively increasing number of live HDPCs with spindle-like morphologies is found for 5B5T, 1MABet4B5T, and 3MABet2B5T, with the culture time from day 1, 3, to 5, whereas only a small number of live cells are detected in 5MABet5T, which agrees with the CCK-8 assay results above. Furthermore, the surface coverage of live cells of these materials was quantitatively determined with Image J software (Fig. 6c) on the basis of their fluorescent images, which displays similar results as the OD values (Fig. 6a). Among three experimental groups, the 1MABet4B5T produces the highest surface coverage of live cells at each period.

The antibacterial effect of the representative dental resins, 5B5T and 1MABet4B5T, were explored against S. mutans by the plate counting method. The small white dots on the culture plates in the digital images ( Fig. 7a) represent the surviving colonies of S. mutans. The denser colonies are observed on 5B5T in the parallel experiments, whereas a significantly decreased number of S. mutans is found on 1MABet4B5T. The quantitative evaluation of CFUs counts (Fig. 7b) shows that the bacterial concentration of the 1MABet4B5T resin is only 0.35 × 108 CFU/mL, much lower than that of 5B5T (7.6 ×108 CFU/mL). The 3D CLSM images of live/dead bacteria (Fig. 7c) indicate that a larger number of dead bacteria is found on 1MABet4B5T whereas almost no dead S. mutans on 5B5T. Their corresponding dead/live bacteria ratio (Fig. 7d) also confirms stronger antibacterial activity of 1MABet4B5T. FE-SEM was further applied to evaluate the structural-morphological changes of S. mutans on different dental resins. More aggregation of S. mutans is observed on 5B5T (Fig. 7e, f), whereas the bacterial adhesion on 1MABet4B5T is effectively prohibited (Fig. 7g, h). Based on the results in Figs. 3–7, the proposed hypothesis was proven.

Bis-GMA is the most commonly used monomer in the field of dentistry, but the potentially estrogenic bisphenol A released from dental materials remains a concern [9–11]. In an attempt to address this issue, the plant-derived betulin was selected as the raw bio-based diols to develop the alternative replacement for Bis-GMA. In this present study, polymerizable dimethacrylate functional groups are further introduced through a facile esterification reaction between betulin and maleic anhydride to synthesize MABet as an alternative monomer for partial or total substitution of Bis-GMA.

During the treatment of dental cavities, the rheology behavior of resin composites is of great importance since it greatly affects the outcomes of restorations [36]. Viscosity is a key parameter influencing differences in the formulations of resin mixtures [34,37]. As presented in Fig. 2, the viscosity of the formulated dental resins is proportional to the concentration of MABet. These viscosity changes can be explained by several reasons. With respect to the structural differences in monomers, the developed MABet, as a diester derivate of betulin, leads to the expression of intermolecular forces including hydrogen bonding and hydrophobic-hydrophobic interactions [18,23,38], which is responsible for the exponential increase in the viscosity of dental resins with increasing the amount of MABet. In addition, MABet has higher molecular weight (637 g/mol) than that of Bis-GMA (512 g/mol) [6], which also matters [20].

Light transmittance is essential to understand the esthetic characteristics and the photopolymerization reactivity of dental resins [39,40]. The effect of MABet on the light transmittance of 1MABet4B5T, 3MABet2B5T, and 5MABet5T was further investigated. It is clearly found that the light transmittance of experimental resin mixtures demonstrates a gradually decreasing trend with increasing MABet addition (Fig. 3a-c). This phenomenon occurs as it is attributed to the light-yellow color of the as-synthesized MABet monomer, which restricts the light penetration during the reaction of the light-polymerization of dental resins [32,33], especially for 5MABet5T. In contrast, the control 5B5T resin without MABet achieves the highest light transmittance. The concerns about the color of the formulated MABet-based resins could be addressed by the use of coloring agents, such as ferric oxide (red), ferric hydroxide (yellow) [41–43], and titanium dioxide (white) [44,45] to allow a more esthetic transition with natural teeth.

The polymerization conversion of dental resin formulations is essential in assessing their physicochemical performance. In the free radical polymerization of dimethacrylate-based dental resins, the double bond conversion is rarely complete by reasons of immobilization, gelation, vitrification and/or steric isolation [46–48]. The residual unpolymerized components might cause cytotoxicity concerns during their service life [49]. The real-time double bond conversion curves of all dental resins tend toward balance over time during the visible-light polymerization (Fig. 3d), resulting from a decrease in the quantity of active free radicals [50]. More importantly, increasing the concentration of MABet in resin mixtures results in lower conversion values at each observation point (Fig. 3d, e). Especially, at the polymerization time of 60 s, the polymerization conversion follows the order of 5B5T > 1MABet4B5T > 3MABet2B5T > 5MABet5T (Fig. 3e). Although MABet4B5T is comparable to 5B5T, all conversion values are lower than 55%, which is the minimum value required from a clinical standpoint [51]. In fact, these findings are directly related to the viscosity behavior of resins. That is, a highly viscous resin slows the movement of the polymer chains during the polymerization reaction, resulting in an earlier gel point and lower conversion values [52,53].

Considering the relatively lower polymerization conversions of the studied dental resins, the composition of residual monomers released from these resins were further characterized by 1H NMR (Fig. 4), using 75 wt% ethanol solution as the storage medium [54]. For the 5B5T, 1MABet4B5T, and 3MABet2B5T groups, Bis-GMA and TEGDMA are found as the released monomers, since they are the main monomers for these resins [55]. The MABet release is also observed in the latter two resins and the 5MABet5T. The above results demonstrate that the monomer release from the resin-soaking solution at 1 day after polymerization is detected regardless of the polymerization conversion, which agrees with previous work [56]. The quantitative analysis of the residual content of Bis-GMA, TEGDMA, and MABet from dental resins was not performed in this work, which could be further measured by the HPLC method [57], etc.

Mechanical performance is critical parameter of dental resins and relates to the clinical lifespan of the restorations. As seen in Fig. 5(a, c), the increasing addition of MABet from 10 to 50 wt% results in a significant decreasing trend in flexural and compressive strength of the resultant resin mixtures. This phenomenon could be as a result of the polymerization kinetics of the developed dental resins. Briefly, the formulated 1MABet4B5T resin demonstrates the highest degree of monomer-to-polymer conversion among all experimental groups (Fig. 3d, e), leading to improved polymer network structure and mechanical properties, which is consistent with previous literature [58–60]. In addition, similar values of flexural modulus are found between the resin formulations (Fig. 5b), which implies that the restorations filled with the 1MABet4B5T-based composite would possess adequate marginal quality [61]. It is worth mentioning that this optimal 1MABet4B5T resin also exhibits better mechanical performance than 5B5T (Fig. 5), although their polymerization behavior is similar (Fig. 3d, e). From the point view of chemical structures, the synthesized MABet monomer has a rigid multicyclic structure of betulin and the hydrogen bonding, which is conducive to mechanical properties [23,62]. Additionally, the polymerizable MABet molecule can be covalently incorporated into the structure of the resulting polymer networks, which also matters to the improved mechanical performance of 1MABet4B5T. Furthermore, the influence of water storage on flexural properties and compressive strength of these dental resins was explored. From Fig. 5(a-c), it is clearly observed that all resins show somewhat decreased mechanical properties after immersion in distilled water for 24 h, which is resulted from the plasticizing effects of absorbed water [63]. The comparison of the four types of resins remains valid.

The analysis of cell viability of resin materials is essential to evaluate their potential applications in dental materials. The release of potentially harmful chemical substances from the dental resins, such as the residual unreacted monomers and photoinitiators, could result in an inflammatory response and other adverse effects within the oral cavity [64]. As shown in Fig. 6, the influence of the MABet concentration on the in vitro cell viability of dental resin formulations was investigated serving 5B5T as control. The results demonstrate that the partial substitution (10 wt%) of Bis-GMA in dental resins by MABet endows the resulting 1MABet4B5T resin with similar cell viability as 5B5T at each culture time. In contrast, the 5MABet5T resin, where Bis-GMA is completely replaced by MABet, yields the highest cytotoxicity to HDPCs of all materials. These results can be ascribed to the polymerization behavior of these resins. In essence, higher conversion of double bonds implies lower amount of residual monomer release [65–67]. As presented in Fig. 3(d, e), both 5B5T and 1MABet4B5T exhibit similar conversion values during the polymerization process, which are significantly higher than 3MABet2B5T and 5MABet5T, and can thereby achieve better cytocompatibility.

Based on the physicochemical properties of dental resin materials (Figs. 2–5) and the cytocompatibility results (Fig. 6) mentioned above, the 1MABet4B5T resin was selected as the optimal experimental resin for the following in vitro antibacterial experiment, where 5B5T served as the control group. It is reported that S. mutans is considered as the main cariogenic pathogen responsible for the development of dental caries in the complex environment of the oral cavity [68], and thereby is selected to determine the antibacterial activity of 1MABet4B5T and 5B5T. According to the qualitative and quantitative results in Fig. 7, the developed 1MABet4B5T resin with 10 wt% MABet presents much higher antibacterial efficiency than 5B5T, which is highly desirable for dental materials [69,70]. Previously, we used the developed dimethacrylate-functionalized betulin derivative (M2Bet) as comonomer for dental resins and obtained the lowest bacterial concentration of 1.53 × 109 CFU/mL for the 1 M2Bet4B5T resin among all materials [23], which is significantly higher than that of the 1MABet4B5T resin (0.35 ×108 CFU/mL) reported in this present work (Fig. 7b). Since the content of M2Bet and MABet is fixed at 10 wt% for resin mixtures, the differences in their antibacterial results above can be attributed to their chemical structures. Firstly, the methacrylate group was directly conjugated to betulin to form M2Bet previously [23], while herein maleic anhydride was esterified with betulin to prepare MABet involving extended residual moieties, which may change the hydrophobic nature of the resin surface and thereby affects bacterial adhesion [71–73]. In addition, the presence of two carboxyl groups (-COOH) in MABet could dissociate into the negatively charged carboxylate anions that induces the electrostatic repulsion between bacteria cells and prohibits bacterial adhesion [74,75]. Meanwhile, carboxyl groups could block the absorption of trace elements by bacteria to inhibit their proliferation [76].

In summary, the betulin-based maleic diester derivative, that is MABet, was successfully synthesized by a facile esterification reaction with a high yield of 83.6%. The obtained MABet was used to partial or total replacement of Bis-GMA to develop dental resins herein. The chemical structure of MABet and the effect of its concentration on the performance of dental resins were further investigated. When Bis-GMA was completely replaced by MABet, the resulting 5MABet5T resin yielded inferior physicochemical properties, mainly due to its lowest degree of conversion of all materials. On the contrary, 10 wt% MABet made the 1MABet4B5T resin exhibit comparable flowability, not the highest transmittance and DC%, improved mechanical performance, and acceptable cytocompatibility when compared with 5B5T. More especially, the developed 1MABet4B5T resin demonstrated higher antibacterial activity against S. mutans. This study introduces a facile strategy to synthesize betulin-based polymerizable monomer for the development of antibacterial dental resins with comparable physicochemical performance to 5B5T. Further work on optimizing the chemical structure of MABet, such as introducing flexible segments, is underway in our group to increase the flowability of monomers and their concentration in resins so as to totally substitute Bis-GMA. In addition, considering the potential application in oral cavity, the ester-free bonds, including acrylamides, will also be introduced into the structure design to improve the degradation resistance.
